paragraphs.heading: Ice set adrift
paragraphs.text: Drift ice, which is also known as brash ice, is sea ice not attached to the shore or to anything else fixed, such as shoals or grounded icebergs. With nothing holding it, winds and sea currents carry it along, which is where its name comes from. That makes it the opposite of fast ice, which is fastened in place. When drift ice is driven together into one large mass covering more than 70% of the area, it is called pack ice.

paragraphs.heading: Made of floes
paragraphs.text: Drift ice is made up of floes, which are separate pieces of sea ice at least 20 metres across. Floes are sorted by size. Small floes are 20 to 100 metres across, medium ones 100 to 500 metres, and big ones 500 to 2,000 metres. Vast floes span 2 to 10 kilometres, and giant floes are more than 10 kilometres wide.

paragraphs.heading: A hazard for ships and piers
paragraphs.text: Wind and currents can pile the ice up into ridges dozens of metres thick. These ridges are a challenge for icebreakers and for structures built in cold seas. Drift ice rammed against a structure pushes with tremendous force. It can tear the rudders and propellers off ships and shear off strong structures anchored to the shore, such as piers, so these have to be retractable or removable. Ships can also get stuck between floes.

paragraphs.heading: The great polar packs
paragraphs.text: The two major packs are the Arctic one, in the Arctic Ocean, and the Antarctic one, in the Southern Ocean. Both form from seawater in the polar regions. They grow and shrink a great deal as the seasons change. Because huge amounts of water are added to or taken from the oceans and the air, the way these packs behave has a large effect on global changes in climate.

paragraphs.heading: A sight worth travelling for
paragraphs.text: Drift ice can also draw visitors. Each season ice drifts through the Sea of Okhotsk off Hokkaidō's northern shore in Japan, and tourists come to see it. It is also listed among the 100 Soundscapes of Japan. This sea is the farthest south in the Northern Hemisphere that drift ice can be seen.
